details: picklescan before 0.0.22 only considers standard pickle file extensions in the scope for its vulnerability scan. An attacker could craft a malicious model that uses Pickle and include a malicious pickle file with a non-standard file extension. Because the malicious pickle file inclusion is not considered as part of the scope of picklescan, the file would pass security checks and appear to be safe, when it could instead prove to be problematic.

descriptions.value: When curl is instructed to get content using the metalink feature, and a user name and password are used to download the metalink XML file, those same credentials are then subsequently passed on to each of the servers from which curl will download or try to download the contents from. Often contrary to the user's expectations and intentions and without telling the user it happened.

When curl is instructed to download content using the metalink feature, thecontents is verified against a hash provided in the metalink XML file.The metalink XML file points out to the client how to get the same contentfrom a set of different URLs, potentially hosted by different servers and theclient can then download the file from one or several of them. In a serial orparallel manner.If one of the servers hosting the contents has been breached and the contentsof the specific file on that server is replaced with a modified payload, curlshould detect this when the hash of the file mismatches after a completeddownload. It should remove the contents and instead try getting the contentsfrom another URL. This is not done, and instead such a hash mismatch is onlymentioned in text and the potentially malicious content is kept in the file ondisk.

descriptions.description: CWE-306 Missing authentication for critical function

descriptions.value:

cna.title: Gvfs: gvfs-admin socket ownership race permits local root

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in the admin backend of gvfs. The privileged gvfsd-admin daemon changes the ownership of newly created private D-Bus sockets by calling the link-following chown() function on a pathname inside a user-controlled directory. A local attacker can exploit this via a Time-of-Check Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) race condition and exchange the socket pathname with a symbolic link pointing to an arbitrary root-owned file (such as /etc/pam.d/su). The daemon subsequently follows the symlink and changes the ownership of the targeted root-owned file to the attacker's user ID. This allows an authenticated local attacker to modify critical system files, leading to a full local privilege escalation to root.

workarounds.value: To mitigate this issue, adjust Polkit rules to require password authentication to start gvfsd-admin or remove execute permissions of the gvfsd-admin binary to prevent execution.

descriptions.value: curl 7.75.0 through 7.76.1 suffers from a use-after-free vulnerability resulting in already freed memory being used when a TLS 1.3 session ticket arrives over a connection. A malicious server can use this in rare unfortunate circumstances to potentially reach remote code execution in the client. When libcurl at run-time sets up support for TLS 1.3 session tickets on a connection using OpenSSL, it stores pointers to the transfer in-memory object for later retrieval when a session ticket arrives. If the connection is used by multiple transfers (like with a reused HTTP/1.1 connection or multiplexed HTTP/2 connection) that first transfer object might be freed before the new session is established on that connection and then the function will access a memory buffer that might be freed. When using that memory, libcurl might even call a function pointer in the object, making it possible for a remote code execution if the server could somehow manage to get crafted memory content into the correct place in memory.

descriptions.value: curl 7.61.0 through 7.76.1 suffers from exposure of data element to wrong session due to a mistake in the code for CURLOPT_SSL_CIPHER_LIST when libcurl is built to use the Schannel TLS library. The selected cipher set was stored in a single "static" variable in the library, which has the surprising side-effect that if an application sets up multiple concurrent transfers, the last one that sets the ciphers will accidentally control the set used by all transfers. In a worst-case scenario, this weakens transport security significantly.

notes.text: A flaw was found in PCRE2. An out-of-bounds write vulnerability exists in the `pcre2_dfa_match` function due to improper size checking when reusing cached workspace blocks. A remote attacker could exploit this by providing a specially crafted regular expression or a recursive pattern in conjunction with a small heap limit. This could lead to data corruption or potentially arbitrary code execution, compromising the integrity and availability of the system.

notes.text: A flaw was found in PCRE2. An out-of-bounds write vulnerability exists in the `pcre2_dfa_match` function due to improper size checking when reusing cached workspace blocks. A remote attacker could exploit this by providing a specially crafted regular expression or a recursive pattern in conjunction with a small heap limit. This could lead to data corruption or potentially arbitrary code execution, compromising the integrity and availability of the system.

notes.text: Important: An out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the PCRE2 library, specifically within the `pcre2_dfa_match` function, could allow arbitrary code execution. This flaw is exploitable in Red Hat products when processing attacker-controlled regular expressions or when a recursive pattern is used in conjunction with a small, API-set heap limit, making it dependent on specific application usage patterns.

To mitigate this Improper Protection of Alternate Path vulnerability, ensure that secondary execution branches—such as the reuse of cached memory workspaces—enforce the exact same size and boundary checks as the primary memory allocation paths. Limit exposure by preventing untrusted user input from directly controlling PCRE2 regular expressions, and strictly avoid utilizing recursive matching patterns when operating under a low heap limit. Apply a defense-in-depth strategy by validating all inputs comprehensively.

cna.title: Busybox: busybox: dpkg-deb extraction-root escape via per-ar-member deferred symlink flush

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in BusyBox's dpkg-deb archive extraction. The ar archive handler flushes deferred symlinks after each archive member, unlike the tar, cpio, and unzip handlers which flush once after the last member. A specially crafted .deb archive with two data.tar members can exploit this ordering: the first member declares a symlink pointing to an absolute path (e.g., '/'), which is deferred as unsafe but flushed after the first member. The second member declares a regular file whose path traverses the now-live symlink, resulting in a file being written outside the intended extraction directory. This could allow an attacker to write arbitrary files to arbitrary locations when a user extracts a crafted .deb package.

descriptions.description: Improper Link Resolution Before File Access ('Link Following')

cna.x_redhatCweChain: CWE-59: Improper Link Resolution Before File Access ('Link Following')

workarounds.value: Do not use BusyBox dpkg-deb to extract untrusted .deb packages. Use Debian's reference dpkg-deb implementation, which treats the extraction root as a boundary and is not affected by this issue. If BusyBox dpkg-deb must be used, inspect .deb archives for multiple data.tar members before extraction (legitimate .deb packages contain exactly one data.tar member).

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Shubham Raj (Causal Security) for reporting this issue.

cna.title: Busybox: busybox: http request smuggling via pipelined requests in httpd reverse proxy

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in BusyBox httpd's reverse proxy feature. When the proxy is configured to forward requests matching a URL prefix to a backend server, only the first HTTP request on a TCP connection has its path rewritten. An attacker can send a pipelined second request that is relayed verbatim to the backend, bypassing the configured path restrictions. This allows accessing arbitrary paths on the backend server that were not intended to be exposed through the proxy.

descriptions.description: Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests ('HTTP Request/Response Smuggling')

cna.x_redhatCweChain: CWE-444: Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests ('HTTP Request/Response Smuggling')

workarounds.value: Do not use BusyBox httpd P: rules as the sole path-based access control in front of sensitive backends. Remove P: lines if proxying is not required, or place a full reverse proxy (for example nginx or HAProxy) in front of the backend. Recompile with FEATURE_HTTPD_PROXY disabled if the applet is not needed.

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Shubham Raj (Causal Security) for reporting this issue.

cna.title: Gstreamer1-plugins-base: gst-plugins-base: heap buffer overflow via unvalidated gstvideometa plane extents in gst_video_frame_map_id and video_meta_deserialize

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in gst-plugins-base. A heap buffer overflow can be triggered when processing video buffers whose attached GstVideoMeta metadata declares plane strides and offsets that exceed the actual backing memory allocation. The metadata is not range-checked during deserialization, and the video frame mapping code does not verify that the declared plane geometry fits within the buffer before allowing consumers to read or write video data. A local attacker who controls the sending side of a GStreamer inter-process IPC pipeline can deliver a crafted buffer carrying fabricated strides, causing the receiving process to read or write beyond heap boundaries. Successful exploitation can cause a denial of service or potentially allow code execution within the affected process.

workarounds.value: If inter-process video sharing via unixfd is not required, build or deploy GStreamer without the unixfd plugin (for example meson option -Dgst-plugins-bad:unixfd=disabled, or omit libgstunixfd.so from the GStreamer plugin directory). Upstream confirms this is the only practical mitigation for the cross-process attack path and notes the unixfd plugin is not currently used by Red Hat-packaged or major distribution software. Operational policy to avoid connecting receiver pipelines to Unix socket endpoints controlled by untrusted local processes provides equivalent protection without rebuilding. This does not address the underlying validation gap in libgstvideo when attacker-controlled GstVideoMeta is supplied in-process.

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Yehia Ezzat (Independent researcher) for reporting this issue.
